Line 1 (p.4b, l.1): For the teacher (*ācārya*) and the spiritual sons (*sādhakaputra*), the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) should be performed together with the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*); for the initiate (*samayin*), it is devoid of that. Line 2:

Even for an initiate who seeks initiation into *nirvāṇa*, [the rite] should be performed by the teacher for the deceased disciple whose body has been cremated and who has attained initiation, provided the [paths] have not yet been traversed. Line 3: It should be performed together with the purification of the paths for one who has passed away.

Having bathed the Śiva-yogin according to the prescribed rite and adorned him with funeral bed-cloths and ornaments, he should place him upon a sacrificial tree prepared in Avantikā. Having secured his two big toes and placed him upon a painted celestial chariot (*citra-vimāna*), accompanied by initiates of the same caste who wear their sacred threads over the left shoulder and recite the *astra-mantra*, and followed by kinsmen amidst the sounds of musical instruments, he should reach the cremation ground at Kaṭodaka in the north-easterly direction.

Having lowered the southern head [of the altar], in that southern enclosure... (p. 5a, l. 1) having constructed a square fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a single girdle (*mekhalā*) six *aṅgulas* in width and height, situated in the east and so forth as appropriate; then, in the northwest corner of that [pit], a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) one cubit wide and six *aṅgulas* high; and in the southeast of the pit, a platform (*vedī*) four *aṅgulas* wide and eight *aṅgulas* deep—or six *aṅgulas* deep, decreasing by one-quarter toward the north—having thus prepared it for the purpose of the seat of the supreme weapon (*astravaradhanyāsana*) which is the foundation of consciousness (*cidādhāta*).

One should smear all of that with cow dung. Then, the Guru, having performed the additional rites of bathing and having adorned himself with the sacred ash-line (*bhasmasūtra*), the crown (*makuṭa*), and other ornaments, shall summon the disciple and perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). [He should do so] for this deceased person here, who is joined with the special initiation of the observance (*samaya-viśeṣa-dīkṣā*), who belongs to the lineage of Śiva (*śiva-gotra*), and who has assumed the form of a preta; following the initiation of Śiva... (l. 7).

For the purpose of removing the fault of deficiency in the practice of the Śaiva rule (*samaya*) as previously described, for the purpose of liberation from the state of being a *preta* or *piśāca*, for the purpose of attaining the aforementioned state, and for the purpose of all expiations (*prāyaścitta*), I shall perform the final rite of the rule (*samayāntyeṣṭi*) according to the procedure taught in the scriptures.

Then, having bathed and performed the ritual of the *sakalīkaraṇa*, the Guru takes the *astravardhanī* [water vessel], proceeds clockwise to the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) facing north, sits upon a seat of *kuśa* grass prepared there in a gentle posture, and dispels the obstacles with the *Pāśupata* [mantra].

Having made the resolve (*saṅkalpya*), having performed the reverse placement (*viparītanyāsa*), and having prepared the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*); (l. 3) having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa as the precursor and having caused the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; having sprinkled the sacrificial hall with the waters of the *puṇyāha* while reciting the *astra-mantra*; (l. 4) having purified and washed the reverse [placement] on the surface and the back with the *astra-mantra*; (l. 5) having placed the seat and the form upon the two surfaces of the painting, starting from the little finger to the thumb, and from the *sadyojāta* face to the *īśāna* face; and having placed the *vidyā-deha*, the eyes, and the root mantras.

Having placed the *hṛdaya* and other mantras on the little finger and the rest, and having enveloped [the body] with the invincible armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should perform the purification of the body by means of the supreme [mantra]. ...

Having visualized the *suṣumnā*, which is of two forms from the anus up to the bladder, of a single form upward to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*), joined at the heart, throat, and other places with the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*, and possessing the form of a hollow tube joined with downward-facing lotus buds.

Having visualized the power (*śakti*) in the form of the supreme void, which flows outward as a stream of nectar, one should [visualize] the blazing syllable *huṃ* in the center. Having performed the *kṛmbha* [mudrā], one should fix the mind upon the *huṃ* and exhale the breath upward.

By means of continuous exhalation, one should cause the lotus buds to turn upward and their knots to be severed. Then, having turned back and exhaled through the right channel (*piṅgalā*), one should again, by means of the inhaled breath (*pūraka*), withdraw the consciousness that was residing in the heart-lotus.

Having placed upon the head the syllable *huṃ*, which has the form of a shimmering star, consists of a peaceful seed-syllable, and is encapsulated within the heart by the individual soul (*jīva*); and having meditated upon the subtle person who has become a drop (*bindu*), solitary and free from affliction, whose body is the seed-syllable, who resides within the crest of the *huṃ*, and who is delimited by eight suns.

Having performed the *kumbhaka* [retention of breath], causing the vital air (*vāyu*) to move upward, and assuming the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should, by means of a single *udghāta* [upward thrust] according to the sequence of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, join [the self] to Śiva at the *dvādaśānta* for the sake of experiencing the karma that is to be experienced, reciting: *oṃ haṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ huṃ ātmane namaḥ*.

Thus, by means of the function of the seed-syllables, one who is absorbed in Śiva should, for the purification of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), cause the principles (*tattvas*) to dissolve in their respective causes in reverse order, up to the *bindu*. That is to say: earth into smell, water into taste, fire into form, wind into touch, and ether into sound—these being the subtle elements (*tanmātras*). These dissolve into the *ahaṅkāra* of darkness (*tāmasa*). The organs called speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals dissolve into the *ahaṅkāra* of passion (*rājasa*). Those called hearing, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose, along with the mind (*manas*), dissolve into the *ahaṅkāra* of goodness (*sāttvika*). That [ahaṅkāra] dissolves into the intellect (*buddhi*); the principle of qualities (*guṇatattva*) into the qualities; and the principle of nature (*prakṛti*) into passion (*rāga*), knowledge (*vidyā*), and power (*kalā*).

Having contemplated that the principles of *puṃstattva*, *kāla*, *niyati*, and *kalā* are thus dissolved into *māyā*; one should contemplate that the principle of *śuddhavidyā* dissolves into the principle of *īśvara*, that into the principle of *sadāśiva*, that into the principle of his *śakti*, and that [the power] into the principle of *śiva*, which is of an undisturbed nature.

One should contemplate it as dissolved into the *bindu*. ... By the utterance of the *prāsāda* [mantra], there is the abandonment of sound and the other [objects of the senses] in the locations beginning with the heart; namely: one should abandon sound and touch in the [lotus] of Brahmā; one should abandon taste in that of Keśava; one should abandon form and smell in that of Rudra; and the intellect (*buddhi*) and ego (*ahaṅkāra*) in that of Īśvara.

One should abandon the mind-drop as Śiva and purify the gross body. For instance: the earthly mandala is yellow, solid, marked with a thunderbolt, presided over by the lord Sadyojāta through the earthly seed-syllable *hām*, joined with Brahmā, the Lord of Causes, and having the form of the *nivṛtti* kalā.

Visualize [the body] as a square, starting from the feet up to the head. Reciting "Oṃ hāṃ nivṛttikalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ" preceded by inhalation (*pūraka*), one should impel the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) through the *suṣumnā* until the end of the twelve [finger-breadths]. Having turned back, one should expel it through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*).

By means of five blows (*udghāta*), having removed the qualities of smell, taste, form, and touch, one should contemplate the earth—overpowered by its own opposite, the wind—as being of that [wind's] form.

Following that—one should contemplate the watery mandala (l. 3), resembling a half-moon, gentle, white, and adorned with lotuses; presided over by the lord Vāmadeva with the watery seed-syllable *hvīṃ* (l. 4); joined with Viṣṇu as the Lord of Causes; having the nature of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā; and extending from the feet up to the crown of the head.

(1.5) *Oṃ hvīṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai haḥ ṅumphah*—having thus, preceded by inhalation (*pūraka*), impelled the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) through the *suṣumnā* as far as the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), and having returned, one should exhale (*virecayet*) through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*). By means of these four upward thrusts (*udghāta*), one should expel the qualities of taste, form, touch, and sound, and contemplate [the element] as being overcome by its own contrary, fire, while endowed with its [fire's] form.

Then the Āgneya-maṇḍala—(p. 8a, l. 1) ... red, adorned with svastikas; presided over by the Lord of the Vidyā-kalā through the seed-syllable of fire, *hrūṃ*, and by Aghora; joined with Rudra, the Lord of Causes; having meditated upon it in the form of the Vidyā-kalā from the feet up to the crown of the head; [one should recite] *oṃ hrūṃ vidyākalāyai haḥ hūṃ phaṭ* while performing inhalation (*pūraka*) through the *suṣumṇā*.

Having impelled the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) as far as the *dvādaśānta* and then returning it, one should expel it through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*). Thus, by means of three upward thrusts (*udghāta*), having cast out the qualities of form, touch, and sound, one should contemplate the fire as being overwhelmed by its own contrary, water, and assume its [water's] form.

Afterwards, [one should visualize] a hexagonal maṇḍala of Vāyu, marked with six *bindus*, black in color, presided over by the seed-syllable of Vāyu, namely *aim*. Then, having meditated upon it as being endowed with the Lord Īśvara—the form of the *kalā* of Peace (*śānti*)—as before, one should impel the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) through the *suṣumnā* up to the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), preceded by inhalation (*pūraka*), while reciting: *oṃ haiṃ... kalāyai haḥ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Having turned back, one should expel [the breath] through the right channel; thus, by means of two *udghātas*, having removed the quality of touch, one should contemplate the form of that touch—which is the wind—overcome by its own obstructing wind.

Thereafter, one should contemplate the mandala of space, which has the form of the sky, resembling pure crystal, empty, adorned with the *bindu* and *śakti*, accompanied by the Lord Sadāśiva—the sovereign cause—who is the Lord Īśāna presiding over the seed-syllable of space, *HAUM*. Having contemplated this, consisting of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*), starting from the feet up to the crown of the head.

Oṃ hauṃ śāntyatītakalāyai haḥ hūṃ phaṭ! Having first performed inhalation (*pūraka*) and impelled the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) through the *suṣumnā* as far as the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), and having returned and exhaled through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*), one should thus expel the quality of sound (*śabdaguṇa*) by means of a single upward thrust (*udghāta*).

Having abandoned its own nature characterized by impermanence, impurity, and so forth, one should meditate upon that very nature as being pervaded by the supreme space (*paramākāśa*), endowed with permanence, omnipresence, purity, and other such qualities. Then, having burned away the defects of the elements residing in the body—initiated by the fire arising from the big toe—with the *astra* [mantra], one should flood it [with water].

Then, having meditated upon the form of the bond as being entirely empty (*sarvaśūnya*), one should flood the entire body—both external and internal—with streams of nectar flowing downward from the *sruc* held at the top of the crest-lock by means of the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, which have entered through the openings of all the channels (*nāḍī*). Having established the seat consisting of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) in the form of a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp by means of the *praṇava* joined with three measures (*mātrā*), and having meditated upon the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city) as descended into its pericarp by means of the *praṇava* with four measures; [one should proceed].

Having established the seed-form of Śiva as the void (*vyomāna*) by means of the five-fold *praṇava* and the inhalation (*pūraka*), one should visualize him as having the form of light; then, by uttering the mantra of Śakti ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should consecrate the unshaken Śakti, who is pervading [the space], with a stream of nectar.

Thereafter, having projected the seat and the form with the heart-mantra; having projected the Brahmās, beginning with Sadyojāta, upon the feet, the secret place, the heart, the mouth, and ending at the crown; having projected the Netra and Mūla mantras upon the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*); and having projected the Heart and other limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) upon the locations beginning with the heart—having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) clockwise three times with the mantra— [End of excerpt]

With the root mantra, one should display the great mudrās. Then, having performed the internal worship, the fire offering, meditation, and the purification of the site by means of the path of withdrawal (*saṃhāramārga*), one should prepare the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*) according to the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta. Having consecrated it with the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should sprinkle the ritual substances with that water. For the sake of illuminating the self, one should [worship] the desired self.

One should perform the purification of the mantras through the process of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*), and having meditated upon Śiva together with Brahmā and his limbs (*aṅga*), one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*). Then, having conceived the six hundred and forty [syllables] by way of the path of withdrawal, one should place the seat (*āsana*) and the form (*mūrti*) in the center of the palm of the right hand, smeared with fragrance, using the left thumb. Having placed the five [faces], beginning with Sadyojāta, on the little finger and so forth, and having performed the placement of the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) and the rest, one should carry out the placement of the eyes (*netra*).

Having invoked Śiva, having placed the mantras of the heart and so forth upon the little finger and the other fingers, having rendered him supreme and having raised him onto one’s own head, one should shake off the veil of darkness—both external and internal—with the splendor that has entered the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Having contemplated the quarters of space as fully illuminated and having remembered Śiva, [one should prepare] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) according to the rule...

Having prepared a nine-square grid on that sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), [one should assign: "Oṃ, obeisance to the square of the *kāla-tattva* in the west"—thus for the square. (p.10b, l.1) "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel consisting of nectar"—thus for the vessel. Therein, one should apply cow dung five times with the *sadyojāta* mantra. "Obeisance to the square of the *puruṣa-tattva* in the north. (l.2)

Thus, for the square: "Oṃ, obeisance to the vessel of jewel-water. Thus, for the vessel. Therein, one should place cow’s urine with the *vāmadeva* mantra four times. To the right: "Obeisance to the square of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*). Thus, for the square. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel possessing splendor. Thus, for the vessel. Therein, one should place clarified butter three times with the *aghora* mantra.

To the eastern cell of the Sadāśiva-tattva, *namaḥ*. Thus [is] the cell. To the vessel of Suśāntaka, *namaḥ*. Thus [is] the vessel. Therein, curd is offered twice with the Tatpuruṣa mantra. In the center, to the cell of the Śiva-tattva, *namaḥ*. Thus [is] the cell. *Oṃ hāṃ*, to the vessel of Supratiṣṭha, *namaḥ*. Thus [is] the vessel.

There, having consecrated the milk once with the Īśāna mantra: "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the cell of the primordial principle (*prakṛti-tattva*) in the northeast," [he places] the cell. "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel of the unmanifest (*avyakta-pātra*)," [he places] the vessel. There, having likewise consecrated the water with *kuśa* grass sixteen times with the root mantra, [he places] the cow-dung and other materials at the end by way of reabsorption (*saṃhāra-mārga*).

Having mixed *kuśa* water with the root mantra, and having again formed a loop with the *kuśa* grass while reciting the *saṃhita* [mantra], one should protect it. Having performed the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) and the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), one should perform the nectar-empowerment (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). Regarding the matter of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should consecrate [the water] one hundred and eight times with the root mantra. Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial hall (*yāgagṛha*) with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and water using the weapon mantra (*astra*), [one should proceed].

Having turned toward the northeast in the southwest, one should scatter ashes and sesame seeds with the *astra-mantra*. Having established the *vardhanī* vessel upon the pedestal in the northeastern square for the purpose of the seat, and having placed it there, one should worship the *cid-āvasatha* (the abode of consciousness). There, having produced twenty-five squares by means of six lines drawn from east to north, [one should proceed].

In the five central squares within the water [mandala], having applied red powder: "Obeisance to the earth element; obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the earth element. In the eight squares of the southwest [corner], having applied white [powder]: "Obeisance to the water element; obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the water element."

In the four squares of the southeast, adorned with red powder: "Obeisance to the element of fire; obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the element of fire. In the four squares of the northwest, adorned with black powder: "Obeisance to the element of wind; obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of the element of wind."

In the four squares of the Īśāna [corner], adorned with green powder: "Obeisance to the element of space (ākāśa-tattva). Obeisance to Sadāśiva, the lord of the element of space. In the eastern square, adorned with yellow powder: "Obeisance to Indra. In the southern square, endowed with black powder: "Obeisance to Yama."

"To Varuṇa, salutation, in the western quarter, accompanied by white powder; to Kubera, salutation, in the northern quarter, accompanied by red powder. Having thus worshipped them in this sequence with perfumes and other offerings, one should present the bali-offering of black-gram flour and so forth, ending with the word *svāhā*. Afterwards, from the northeast, [the offering is made] upon the *vikara* of withdrawal.

In the *vardhanī* vessel filled with water and provided with thread and cloth as before, having stationed the *pāśupatāstra*, [one should recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to the seat of Ananta; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the foundational power (*mūlādhāra-śakti*). In the corners starting from the northeast and ending with the southeast: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); obeisance to Dispassion (*vairāgya*)."

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Knowledge; homage to Dharma. (L. 4) In the directions starting from the north and ending with the east: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Sovereignty of Mind; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Non-Dispassion; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ignorance; (L. 5) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Non-Dharma. In the corners of Nairṛti, Īśāna, and Aghora, and below, [homage] to Candra.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the upward-facing moon. (l. 6) In the center, homage to the lotus. Oṃ haṃ, homage to the seed-syllables. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the pericarp. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the filaments. (p. 12b, l. 1) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the petals. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the stalk. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the sprout. (l. 2) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the weapon-seat, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the weapon-form, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
Resplendent like ten million suns, with a roar like the clouds at the end of an aeon. (l. 2)
Three-eyed, with a serpent as his sacred thread, four-faced, and four-armed.
With his teeth, beard, and hair ablaze, holding a spear,
a mallet, a trident, and a sword in his hands, and adorned with a crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Having meditated thus: *Oṃ śiṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. Having thus invoked [the deity], [one should offer worship with]:
*Oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *Oṃ klīṃ śirase huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *Oṃ paṃ śikhāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*;
*Oṃ śuṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *Oṃ huṃ netrebhyo huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *Oṃ phaṭ astrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.

Having thus performed the ritual identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the limbs and [performed] the invocation (*āvāhana*) and all other services (*upacāra*), one should visualize the pavilion as having all obstacles entirely dispelled by splendors. Then, in the pitchers situated in the directions beginning with the northeast—specifically in the northeast pitcher—one recites: *oṃ hāṃ triśūlāsanāya namaḥ* (Homage to the trident-seat); *triśūlamūrttaye namaḥ* (Homage to the embodiment of the trident).

The divine person of the trident, whose body is the entire sky... (l. 2). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one who shines with the trident. In the northern jar, in the jar: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the mace. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the mace. Among the maidens of the radiant light of the mace, [the syllables] pi-ja-ghna-sta-lā*—Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the mace. (l. 4)

In the northwest corner, upon the pitcher: *oṃ hāṃ dhvajāsanāya namaḥ* | *oṃ hāṃ dhvajamūrttaye namaḥ* | The Banner (*dhvaja*) is green like Varuṇa, with a wide-open mouth and great arms; [one should worship] the Banner: *dhvajāya namaḥ* | [Having worshipped], in the west: *oṃ hāṃ pāśāsanāya namaḥ* | *oṃ hāṃ pāśamūrttaye namaḥ* |

[One should worship] that which is endowed with seven hoods and a noose, joined with a human head; *oṃ hāṃ pāśāya namaḥ*. [Jyeṣṭhā]. In the southwest (*naiṛta*): *oṃ hāṃ khaḍgāsanāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ khaḍgamūrttaye namaḥ*. And the sword [is worshipped]; [it is] dark blue in body, with eyes like a thunderbolt; *oṃ hāṃ khaḍgāya namaḥ*. [Jyeṣṭhā]. In the south: *oṃ hāṃ daṇḍāsanāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍamūrti. Daṇḍa is also a person, dark-complexioned with copper-red eyes. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍa. [In the] south-east: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śaktyāsana. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śaktimūrti. Śakti has the form of a woman, made of copper... Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śakti. [In the] south-east. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā.

In the east: *Oṃ hāṃ*, homage to Vajrāsana; *Oṃ hāṃ*, homage to Vajramūrti. [The deity is] a person, gross, hard, firm, and flowing... *Oṃ hāṃ*, homage to Vajra. *Jya*. In the northwest and north, in the pitcher: *Oṃ hāṃ*, homage to Cakrāsana; *Oṃ hāṃ*, homage to Cakramūrti. A hundred-spoked wheel, with *Bhṛṃ* at the head, powerful, dark-blue... measuring.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Discus (Cakra). In the southern jar of Īśāna: Oṃ hāṃ, Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lotus Throne (Padmāsana). (l. 4) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lotus-Formed One (Padmamūrti). [He is] the Lotus-Man, with divine white limbs and auspicious eyes. (l. 5) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lotus (Padma). Since you have indeed spoken of the weapons that protect the quarters and the ritual of the bricks (iṣṭikarma), let it be told; now, let the command of Śiva be proclaimed together.

Then, on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), having fashioned lotuses with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains, it should be resplendent with royal ashes. On the jar, there should be the seven kinds of grain; or else, having prepared kuśa grass, ashes, and sesame seeds upon the sacrificial ground, which is beautified by all splendors, one should worship the gate-keepers and others with the *astra-mantra* and the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) according to the prescribed marks.

As before, in the center: *namaḥ* to Ādhāraśakti; *namaḥ* to Anantāsana. In the corners: *namaḥ* to Aiśvarya; *namaḥ* to Vairāgya; *namaḥ* to Jñāna; *namaḥ* to Dharma. *Oṃ*, in the northern directions: *namaḥ* to Anaiśvarya; *namaḥ* to Avairāgya; *namaḥ* to Ajñāna; *namaḥ* to Adharma. [In the corners] between Nairṛti and Īśāna: [as above].

Salutation to Adaś-candana; salutation to Ūrdhva-candana; salutation to the lotus in the center; salutation to the seeds; salutation to the pericarp; salutation to the [petals]; salutation to the leaves; salutation to the stalk; salutation to the sprout; salutation to the bulb; in the northeast of the pericarp, salutation to Manonmanī.

In the filaments beginning with Īśāna and ending with the East: *namaḥ* to Sarvabhūtadamanī; *namaḥ* to Balapramathanī; *namaḥ* to Balavikaraṇī; *namaḥ* to Kalavikaraṇī; *namaḥ* to Kālī; *namaḥ* to Raudrī; *namaḥ* to Jyeṣṭhā; *namaḥ* to Vāmā. In the center of the pericarp: *namaḥ* to the Śakti-maṇḍala; *namaḥ* to the Lord of the Śakti-maṇḍala.

Homage to Īśvara; homage to the fire-maṇḍala on the circle at the tip of the pericarp; homage to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala. Homage to the moon-maṇḍala on the circle at the tips of the filaments; homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the moon-maṇḍala. Homage to the sun-maṇḍala on the circle at the tips of the petals.

Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc. Above that: *oṃ hāṃ* salutation to the seat of Śiva; *oṃ hāṃ* salutation to the form of Śiva. From the feet to the top of the head: *oṃ haṃ* salutation to the Sadyojāta form; *oṃ giṃ* salutation to the secret organ of Vāmadeva; *oṃ huṃ* salutation to the Aghora form; *oṃ heṃ* salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should meditate: ...in the mouth [is] the jar, the person, the foot, and Śiva seated upon the throne, red in color, with five lotus-faces.
He has ten arms and three eyes; in each right hand he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and a vajra.
Holding fire and a noose to the left, and in that same sequence holding a bell, a staff, and a goad;

[reciting] *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ vidyādehāya namaḥ*. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the five faces and eyes with *oṃ hauṃ netrebhyo namaḥ* on the faces beginning with Sadyojāta, and having filled the hollowed palms (*añjali*) with flowers, one should invoke Śiva with the root mantra. Then, having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and firm fixation (*sannirodhana*).
O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World, until the end of the final dissolution,
may you remain present within this jar with a spirit of affection.
O Śambhu, O Lord, by your command the funeral rites for this deceased man shall be performed; O Supreme Lord, be gracious so that he may attain your state.

Having thus made this request, and having offered the guest-water (*svāgatārghya*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and the other mantras upon the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the hands. Having established oneness [with the deity] by means of the root-mantra, one should protect [the deity] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and enclose [him] counter-clockwise with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*). Having displayed the nectar-gesture (*amṛtamudrā*), one should consecrate [the deity] as supreme by means of the great-gesture (*mahāmudrā*) with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Having filled [the vessel] with the five-faced gesture (*pañcamukhīmudrā*), one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and guest-water (*arghya*). Then, [one should perform] the anointing, rubbing with unguents, bathing, and so forth.

Having visualized the components of the ritual ablution (*snapanāṅga*), having bathed [the deity] with drops of *arghya* water, and having wiped [him] with a fine cloth, one should mentally offer with devotion sandalwood paste, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), dūrvā grass, gold, a loincloth (*kaupīna*), a girdle (*mekhalā*), a sacred thread (*upavīta*), earrings, ornaments, and variegated garments.

With three handfuls of flowers, [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ namo śivāya ātmatattvādhipataye* (Salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of the self). *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ namo śivāya vidyātattvādhipataye* (Salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of knowledge). *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ namo śivāya śivatattvādhipataye* (Salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of Śiva).

One should display the *manorathamudrā*. Having worshipped the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) with the mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, one should worship the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*). In the west: *namaḥ* to the form of *sadyojāta*. In the north: *namaḥ* to the secret part of *vāmadeva*. In the south: *namaḥ* to the heart of *aghora*. In the east: *namaḥ* to the face of *tatpuruṣa*. In the northeast: *namaḥ* to the head of *īśāna*. To the north of *īśāna*: *hauṃ namaḥ* to the eyes. In the southeast: *namaḥ* to the heart. To the north of the eye: *hīṃ namaḥ* to the head.

In the southwest, *namaḥ* to the *śikhā*; in the northwest, *namaḥ* to the *kavaca*. Having worshipped these, beginning from the north and ending with the east, [one worships] the *astra*. Having consecrated them with the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) as in the case of Śiva, one should worship them.

Having shown the *brahmāṇa*, *śaṅkha*, *triśūla*, *padma*, and *dhenu* mudrās, and the *namaskāra* mudrā for the limbs, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra, one should show the *mahāmudrā* and contemplate the state of oneness with Śiva for all of them.

Then, in the second enclosure, in the directions starting from the northeast and ending with the east: *namaḥ śikhaṇḍine*—*namaḥ śrīkaṇṭhāya*—*namaḥ trimūrtaye*—*namaḥ ekarudrāya*—*namaḥ ekanetrāya*—*namaḥ śivottamāya*—*namaḥ sūkṣmāya*—*namaḥ anantāya*.
In the third enclosure: *namaḥ caṇḍāya*—*namaḥ devyai*—*namaḥ skandāya*—*namaḥ vṛṣabhāya*—*namaḥ vināyakāya*—*namaḥ bhṛṅgine*—*namaḥ mahākālāya*—*namaḥ nandine*.

In the fourth enclosure: salutation to Īśāna; salutation to Kubera; salutation to Vāyu; salutation to Varuṇa; salutation to Nirṛti; salutation to Yama; salutation to Agni; salutation to Indra. In the fifth enclosure: salutation to the trident; salutation to the mace; salutation to the banner; salutation to the noose; salutation to the sword; salutation to the staff; salutation to the spear; salutation to the thunderbolt; salutation to the discus; salutation to the lotus.

Having worshipped these with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, and having performed the worship up to the recitation (*japa*), she is to be honored. (6) Having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and sat down, there, with the root mantra placed by the ring finger and thumb, one should gaze at the pit with the eye; sprinkle it with the *Śiva-mantra*; strike it with *kuśa* grass using the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; sprinkle it with the *kavaca-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*; and perform digging, scattering, filling, sprinkling, pouring, and pounding.

Having performed the sweeping and smearing with a sword or *kuśa* grass, and having blunted [the blade], [one should worship] in the northwest, south, east, and center: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛttikalā. Oṃ hvīṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhākalā. Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Vidyākalā. Oṃ hyaiṃ, obeisance to Śāntikalā. Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śāntyatītākalā. Having thus conceptualized [the pit] as consisting of the *kalās*, and having encircled it with a triple-thread using the weapon-mantra, one should worship it with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the pit consisting of the *kalās*."

Drawing four lines extending southward or westward along with the transverse line, one forms a trident shape on both sides. Using three *kuśa* blades, one performs the *vajrīkaraṇa* (diamond-making). With two hands whose fingers point toward the east and north, one lays down four footprints within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) using the *astra-mantra*. Having arranged the *kuśa* grasses with their stalks intact according to the prescribed rite, one places in the center a bundle of *kuśa* in the form of a brush (*kūrca*). Reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara," the wise practitioner should duly invoke the Goddess upon that seat.

Having meditated upon Viśvāmātṛ, who is dark-complexioned, in her fertile state, adorned with excellent garlands of *soma* flowers, with a serene countenance and three eyes resembling lotus petals—having thus meditated, one should worship Vāgīśvarī with perfumes and other offerings, saying: "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. Then, having brought fire from a churning stick or from a flame, O twice-born one, into an earthen vessel or a betel-leaf vessel, [one should proceed].

Having placed [the fire] in the southeast, northeast, or southwest, one should expel a fragment of fire toward the southwest with the Astra-mantra for the sake of the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*). Having purified it through the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, one should take up the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ vahnimūrttaye namaḥ*.

Then, having united it with the heart-mantra, the breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), the fire of the navel, and the fire of the point (*bindu*), one should expel it with the exhalation (*recaka*) and place it in the vessel upon the fire with the mantra: *oṃ hrūṃ vahnicaitanyāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped with the *saṃhitā* [mantra], having protected it by circumambulating counter-clockwise and having veiled it with the *prāsāda* [mantra] ending in *vauṣaṭ*, having rendered it nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā*, and having taken it up, one should whirl it clockwise above the *kuṇḍa*. Meditating on it as the "seed of Śiva" (*śivabīja*), and visualizing the Father [Śiva] with his head turned away, one should contemplate it being deposited into the womb-channel of Vāgīśvarī. Then, with the root of the knee resting on the ground, one should deposit it facing oneself.

Then, having visualized the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) as the lower garment at the region of the navel, one should offer a drop of water for the purpose of purification and sipping with the heart-mantra; cover it with fuel sticks while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*); and kindle it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), saying: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the embryonic fire (*garbhāgni*). Having thus worshipped the embryonic fire, one should tie a bracelet of *darbha* grass consecrated by the weapon-mantra upon the left wrist with the heart-mantra for the protection of the embryo. Then, having worshipped with the Sadyojāta mantra for the sake of the conception of the embryo, one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the heart-mantra.

For the sake of *pumsavana* (ensuring the birth of a male), in the third month, having worshipped with the *Vāmadeva* mantra, one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the head-mantra (*śiraḥ*), and then cast a drop [of clarified butter]. For the sake of the *sīmantonnayana* (parting the hair), in the sixth month, having worshipped with the *Aghora* mantra, one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the crest-mantra (*śikhā*).
One should then contemplate the formation of the face and limbs from the crest itself, as well as the expiation (*niṣkṛti*).

For the sake of giving birth, at the tenth month, the man, having worshipped [the deity] with the *kavaca* mantra, should offer three oblations of sesame seeds. Once the child is born, he should prepare a fire with *darbha* grass and other materials for the purpose of a bath that removes the impurities of the womb. Having removed the *darbha* bracelet from the hand of the Goddess and meditating upon the golden bond made by the Goddess, he should worship it with the *hṛdaya* mantra. Then, for the immediate cessation of the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), [he should purify] the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra.

Having sprinkled [the site] with *darbha* grass, struck it with the *astra-mantra*, and sprinkled it again with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing toward the south and west upon the northern and other girdles (*mekhalā*) for the protection of the fire, using the *astra-mantra*. Upon those [blades], having likewise arranged the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the ritual seats (*viṣṭara*), [one proceeds] for the removal of the saliva from the [fire’s] mouths.

For the sake of the back of the fire and for the root and tip [of the blades], one should offer five fuel-sticks smeared with ghee using a sword, along with parched grain flour (*saktu*) upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). On the north: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvara*. On the south: *obeisance to Rudra*. On the west: *obeisance to Viṣṇu*. On the east: *obeisance to Brahmā*. Upon the seats (*viṣṭara*), [one should worship] Īśāna and the others.

Having worshipped and offered the *arghya* water, one should proclaim the command of Śiva: "You shall split the child. Then, having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with their mouths downward and their handles upward upon the *kuśa* grass, one should sprinkle them with the *astra-mantra*, wash them with the *kavaca-mantra*, enclose them [with the *varma-mantra*], and heat them in the fire.

Having rotated [the blade] and touched its tip with the tip of a *kuśa* grass, having again rotated it and touched the middle with the middle, and having again rotated it and touched the base with the base—at those points touched by the *kuśa*, one should contemplate the three principles (*tattva*) known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, corresponding respectively to Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.

According to the sequence of the *Saṃyuta*: having placed the *sṛci-śakti* [mantra] upon the *śaṃbara*, and having placed the *śambhu* upon the *sruva*; with the *varman* [mantra], the neck is triple-wrapped. Having warmed it over the *kuśa* grass in the north-western direction by means of the root-mantra (*mūla*), one should worship it... Then, having brought the clarified butter (*ājya*) from a cow and purified it through the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, one should contemplate one's own body as consisting of Brahman. Taking it, one should heat it three times counter-clockwise in the vicinity of the fire within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having established it in the south-east (*āgneyī*), one should take a drop from the tip of a *darbha* blade.

Having offered oblations with "Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā," and having again meditated upon one's own body as consisting of Viṣṇu, one should place [the vessel] in the northeast by circumambulation; then, having offered a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave svāhā," one should meditate upon the form of the *paryāsa* as consisting of Rudra.

Holding [the vessel] at the navel, one should offer a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting: "Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Rudra. Having thus concluded the rite, one should take a *pavitraka*—made from two tips of *darbha* grass ten finger-breadths long with a knot in the middle—between the thumb and ring finger, and with the *astra-mantra*, sprinkle the clarified butter, the fire, and the well-faced [deity] three times.

Having performed the *saṃplavana* rite with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) over the *pavitra* blades which have faces turned toward the reality of the self, one should untie that *pavitra*-knot and cast it into the fire. Having thrown the torch (*ulkā*) of burnt *darbha* grass into the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should cast away the *pavitra* blades after heating them with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*). Having ignited [the remaining] blazing *darbha* grass with the armor-mantra and cast it into the fire, and having further kindled the torch with the blazing weapon-mantra, one should throw that heated torch into the fire. Then, having placed two *kuśa* blades with a central knot, each measuring a span (*prādeśa*), into the middle of the clarified butter with the *praṇava* (Om), [one should proceed].

Having visualized the two fortnights, white and black, in sequence from right to left, and having contemplated the three channels—Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Suṣumnā—in the right, left, and middle portions [of the body], one should take clarified butter with the sacrificial ladle from the right side and offer it with: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*. Then, taking clarified butter from the left side, one offers it into the left eye of the fire with: *oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā*. Taking it from the middle, one offers it into the middle eye of the fire with: *oṃ hāṃ agniṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*. And [finally] into the middle eye of the fire with: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*.

Having offered a small portion into the mouth of Agni (*agnivaktra*) with this [mantra], one should cast the remainder into the *ājyabhāga* oblations. Having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *saṃhitā* [mantra], one should protect it. Having veiled it clockwise, one should transform it into nectar (*amṛtīkṛta*) by means of the root mantra and the *dhenumudrā*. Having worshipped it with the root mantra, one should perform the purification of the *bindu*, *kṣveḍa*, *dhanya*, and *ājya*. Thereafter: *Oṃ hāṃ sadyojātāya svāhā |* *Oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya svāhā |* *Oṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā |* *Oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā |* *Oṃ hoṃ īśānāya svāhā |*

Thus one should perform the sprinkling with the mouth: *oṃ haṃ hiṃ sadyojāta-vāmadevābhyāṃ svāhā*. *oṃ hiṃ huṃ vāmadeva-aghorābhyāṃ svāhā*. *oṃ huṃ heṃ aghora-tatpuruṣābhyāṃ svāhā*. *oṃ heṃ hoṃ tatpuruṣa-īśānābhyāṃ svāhā*.

Having thus performed the union with these two [mantras], one should perform the unification of the fire-face with the words: *oṃ haṃ hiṃ huṃ heṃ hoṃ svāhā to Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna*. This is done by means of the [line] going from the fire to the wind and [the line] going from Nirṛti to Īśāna, [using] clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Then, for the purpose of naming [the fire], one should worship with Īśāna. Having offered three oblations with the Astra-mantra, one should give it the name "Śivāgni" (the Fire of Śiva), meaning "Hutāśana" (the Consumer of Oblations). Having worshipped Vāgīśī and Vāgīśvara with the Hṛdaya-mantra, one should dismiss them. Then, having fashioned the mouth [of the fire] according to the desired measurement of the *kuṇḍa*, [one should perform the rite] at the middle tongue... until the end.

For the purpose of completing the ritual action (*saṃskāra*), one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Just as one fills a ladle (*sruc*) with clarified butter and offers it into the fire with the bowl turned downwards, one should place a flower at its tip. Then, with the left and right hands joined like a conch shell, and again joined together by the left hand—

...having risen with feet together and then placing both [feet] sideways on the ground with the knees even, casting his gaze toward the tip of the bow, and uttering the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, he should bring the base of the clay to the end of the left breast and, without hesitation, pour the entire clarified butter into the fire in a stream the size of a barley grain. Having thus performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should sit down. [He should meditate upon the Lord] seated upon a white lotus throne, five-faced and four-armed, with a long beard, possessing a form as described, and with his crest adorned by matted locks (*jaṭā*).

Having thus meditated upon Agni, whose lotus-like hands are occupied with a sacrificial ladle, a water-pot, a staff, and a rosary: "O Agni, since you are the supreme purifying splendor of Īśvara, therefore, having established [the deity] within your heart-lotus, I offer libations."

Having thus offered this prayer, he enters the central channel within the body of Śeṣa. As before, having worshipped the Lord Śiva together with his throne in the heart-lotus using all ritual offerings and having honored the surrounding deities, [he recites]: "Oṃ hāṃ, Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti and the others."

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Anantāsana. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ananta. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Aiśvarya; homage to Vairāgya; homage to Jñāna; homage to Dharma. Homage to Anaiśvarya; homage to Avairāgya; homage to Ajñāna; homage to Adharma.

Salutation to Adhaś-candana; salutation to Ūrdhva-candana. Salutation to the lotus; salutation to the seeds; salutation to the pericarp; salutation to the filaments; salutation to the petals; salutation to the stalk; salutation to the sprout; salutation to the bulb. In the northeast of the pericarp, salutation to Manonmanī.

In the filaments starting from Īśāna and ending with the East: homage to Sarvabhūtadamanī; homage to Balapramathanī; homage to Balavikaraṇī; homage to Kalavikaraṇī; homage to Kālī; homage to Raudrī; homage to Jyeṣṭhā; homage to Vāmā. In the center of the pericarp: homage to the Śakti-maṇḍala.

Salutation to the Lord of the Śakti-maṇḍala; salutation to Īśvara. On the circle at the tip of the pericarp: salutation to the Vahni-maṇḍala; salutation to the Lord of the Vahni-maṇḍala; salutation to Rudra. On the circle at the tips of the filaments: salutation to the Soma-maṇḍala; salutation to the Lord of the Soma-maṇḍala; salutation to Viṣṇu.

On the circumference at the tip of the petals: "Oṃ, salutation to the solar disc. "Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc. Above that: "Salutation to the seat of Śiva; Oṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva. Salutation to Sadyojāta; salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Aghora;
salutation to Tatpuruṣa; salutation to Īśāna.
In the center, within the lotus of the heart, is Śiva seated upon a lotus throne in the fire situated within the sacrificial pit.
The Jewel [Maṇidhara] has a lotus-face, ten arms, and three eyes on each face;
he holds, in order from right to left, a trident, an axe, a sword, and a vajra, as well as fire,
a noose, a bell, a lotus, and a goad.

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to the one whose body is knowledge (vidyādeha). [One should worship] with "Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the eyes" upon the faces beginning with Sadyojāta. Having invoked Śiva by means of the root mantra and performed the rites of installation and presence:
"O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world, until the conclusion of the worship, remain present in this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with a spirit of affection."

Having thus made this request, and having offered the welcome-arghya, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and the other mantras in the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the *kārā* [the crown]. Having established oneness with the root mantra, and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) in a counter-clockwise direction, one should perform the sprinkling (*prakṣaṇa*), protection (*saṃrakṣaṇa*), and the sealing (*avakuṇṭhana*). Then, with the root mantra, one should display the nectar-mudrā (*amṛtamudrā*).

Having clearly manifested the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having bound the Five-Face Seal (*pañcamukhīmudrā*), one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the two feet with the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*. With [the mantra] ending in *svadhā*, one offers water for sipping (*ācamana*) to the five faces beginning with Īśāna. Likewise, having offered the water of honor (*arghya*) to the five heads with [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*, one should present flowers, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth, with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Having performed the mental consecration, having bathed [the deity] with drops of water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), and having wiped away subtle latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one should mentally and with devotion offer sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), *dūrvā* grass, gold, a loincloth, a girdle, a sacred thread, earrings, ornaments, and variegated garments.

Having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers, one should display the *manoratha-mudrā*. Having worshipped the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras, one should worship the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*). [One should offer: "Homage to the form of Sadyojāta in the west; homage to Vāmadeva in the north; homage to Aghora in the south."

In the east: *namaḥ* to Tatpuruṣa. In the northeast: *namaḥ* to Īśāna. To the north of Īśāna: *hauṃ namaḥ* to the Heart (*hṛdaya*) [and to the Eyes (*netra*)]. In the southeast: *namaḥ* to the Heart. To the north of the Eye: *hīṃ namaḥ* to the Head (*śiras*). In the southwest: *namaḥ* to the Crest-lock (*śikhā*). In the northwest: *namaḥ* to the Armor (*kavaca*).

Having worshipped these [deities]—beginning with the north and ending with the east—and having consecrated them with the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) starting with the invocation (*āvāhana*) as one does for Śiva, one should worship them. Having displayed the *brahmā*, *makara*, *triśūla*, *padma*, and *dhenu* mudrās, as well as the *namaskāra* mudrā for the limbs, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should display the *mahāmudrā* and contemplate the oneness of all [the deities] with Śiva.

Then, in the second enclosure, in the directions starting from the northeast and ending with the east: *namaḥ* to Śikhaṇḍin; *namaḥ* to Śrīkaṇṭha; *namaḥ* to Trimūrti; *namaḥ* to Ekarudra; *namaḥ* to Ekanetra; *namaḥ* to Śivottama; *namaḥ* to Sūkṣma; *namaḥ* to Ananta.
In the third enclosure: *namaḥ* to Caṇḍa; *namaḥ* to Devī; *namaḥ* to Skanda; *namaḥ* to Vṛṣabha; *namaḥ* to Vināyaka; *namaḥ* to Bhṛṅgin; *namaḥ* to Mahākāla; *namaḥ* to Nandin.

In the fourth enclosure: obeisance to Īśāna; obeisance to Kubera; obeisance to Vāyu; obeisance to Varuṇa; (l. 4) obeisance to Nirṛti; obeisance to Yama; obeisance to Agni; obeisance to Indra. In the fifth enclosure: (l. 5) obeisance to the trident; obeisance to the mace; obeisance to the banner; obeisance to the noose; obeisance to the sword; obeisance to the staff; obeisance to the spear; obeisance to the thunderbolt; obeisance to the discus; (l. 6) obeisance to the lotus.

Having worshipped these [deities] from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the end of the recitation (*japa*), and having performed the union of the two mouths of Śiva, one should emerge; then, uttering the root mantra, one should cause the flame in the form of light—which has issued from the nostril of the Śiva residing in the fire—to merge into the flame of the Śiva present at the sacrifice.

One should meditate on the severed [connection] caused by the mere separation from the fire, [as if] both agents were blind. Thus, having joined the channel together with the self by means of the jar, the sacrifice, and the fire—having offered three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of the union, and having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra for the sake of satiating the mantra.

Having offered the *pūrṇā* oblation, for the sake of warding off ill omens arising from the country, the materials, or the time, and for the purpose of bringing about auspicious omens, one should offer four hundred oblations with the root mantra according to one's capacity, and perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and illumination (*dīpana*) of the mantra. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ sadyojātamūrtaye svāhā | Oṃ hiṃ vāmadevaguhyāya svāhā | Oṃ huṃ aghorahṛdayāya svāhā | Oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya svāhā | Oṃ hoṃ īśānamūrdhāya svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya svāhā |

Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ haiṃ, svāhā to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to the eyes. Oṃ haḥ, svāhā to the weapon (astra). Thus, one performs the libation with each individual oblation. Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, hum phaṭ to Śiva. Oṃ haṃ huṃ haṃ, hum phaṭ to the Sadyojāta form. Oṃ haṃ hiṃ huṃ, hum phaṭ to the secret [form] of Vāmadeva. Oṃ haṃ huṃ huṃ, hum phaṭ to the heart of Aghora. Oṃ haṃ heṃ huṃ, hum phaṭ to the face of Tatpuruṣa.

Oṃ hūṃ hoṃ hūṃ īśānamūrdhāya hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hūṃ hṛdayāya hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ hūṃ śīrse hūṃ phaṭ | (p.27b, l.1) Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ śikhāyai hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ haiṃ hūṃ kavacāya hūṃ phaṭ | (l.2) Oṃ hūṃ hauṃ hūṃ netrebhyaḥ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ haḥ hūṃ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ | Thus, illumination is performed with three oblations. One should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). In the center of the funeral pyre, having drawn a square with yellow powder and above that three [lines] with red powder, upon those two—

Having worshipped the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) and the fire, one should drive stakes made of dry wood—pointed upwards and facing downwards—into the corners of the altar starting from the southeast (*āgneya*), following the counter-clockwise order (*apasavya-krama*), after consecrating them once with the *astra-mantra*. Then, having encircled the fivefold enclosure with a thread while reciting the *kavaca-mantra*, one should wrap it in a counter-clockwise direction.

Having filled the funeral pyre with sandalwood and other fragrant substances mixed together, and having covered it with a cloth turned inside out, one should worship the *pāśupatāstra* mantra with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and sesame seeds. Then, having bathed the corpse with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), earth, cow dung, goat’s milk, and water, using the *astra* mantra, one should [apply] ashes, *akṣata* grains, and dust to the feet and so forth in successive order, reciting the *sadyojāta* and other mantras.

[Having performed] the rite of past births... (l. 2) ...having made the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), having put on two clean garments, and having adorned [the deceased] with perfumes and other offerings, one should place [him] upon a seat of *kuśa* grass prepared to the left of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)... (l. 4). At this juncture, if the body has been fashioned from *kuśa* grass and other materials, then in the case of initiation for the deceased (*mṛtaka-dīkṣā*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of the thirty-two principles (*tattva*) together with their presiding deities (*sādhipati*). (l. 5)

For example, like the *karavīra* flowers and earrings, the principles (*tattvas*) reside in the subtle body; those intended for that [purpose] are as follows: first, one should install the Lord (*pati*) by means of the emission of the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*). Above the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), [one says]: *oṃ hāṃ tirodhānaśaktaye namaḥ*. At the root-aperture of Brahmā, [one says]: *oṃ hāṃ rodhanaśaktaye namaḥ*.

In the central *brahmarandhra*: *oṃ hāṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ*. To Śiva, the lord of the *śivatattva*, obeisance. In the head (*mūrdhan*): *oṃ hāṃ śaktitattvāya namaḥ*. To Śaktimān, the lord of the *śaktitattva*, obeisance. Above the upper portion of the head: *oṃ hāṃ sadāśivatattvāya namaḥ*. To Brahmā, the lord of the *sadāśivatattva*, obeisance.

On the neck: *oṃ hāṃ* obeisance to the principle of Īśvara (*īśvaratattva*). Obeisance to Ananta, the lord of the principle of Īśvara. ... (l. 5) *oṃ hāṃ* obeisance to the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*). Obeisance to Maheśvara, the lord of the principle of Pure Knowledge. On the right side: *oṃ hāṃ* obeisance to the principle of Māyā (*māyātattva*). (l. 6) *oṃ hāṃ* obeisance to Gahaneśa, the lord of the principle of Māyā.

On the left side: *oṃ hāṃ kālatattvāya namaḥ*; [and] *namaḥ* to Kāla, the lord of the *kālatattva*. In the heart: *oṃ hāṃ niyatitattvāya namaḥ*; *namaḥ* to Niyāmaka, the lord of the *niyatitattva*. In the belly: *oṃ hāṃ kalātattvāya namaḥ*; *namaḥ* to Jñānabindu, the lord of the *kalātattva*.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*); obeisance to the Lord of the principle of knowledge, the one possessing Vedic wisdom. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*); obeisance to the Lord of the principle of passion, the bestower of desire. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the person (*puruṣa-tattva*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the principle of the person, the subtle body (*sūkṣma-deha*). Thus, the group of four [is placed] in the belly.

On the spinal column: *oṃ hāṃ* homage to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*); homage to Pradhāna, the lord of the principle of primordial nature. (L. 6) Within the center of the navel: *oṃ hāṃ* homage to the principle of the qualities (*guṇa-tattva*); homage to Trideha, the lord of the principle of the qualities. In the joints: *oṃ hāṃ* homage to the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*); homage to Buddha, the lord of the principle of intellect. (P. 29b, l. 1)

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāra-tattva*). Homage to Ahaṅkṛti, the lord of the principle of ego. (L. 2) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). Homage to Saṅkalpa, the lord of the principle of mind. In the ear: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of hearing (*śrotra-tattva*). (L. 2) Homage to Vyomacārin, the lord of the principle of hearing.

On the skin: *oṃ hāṃ*, homage to the principle of the skin (*tvaktattva*), homage to the Lord of the principle of the skin, the All-limbed One (*sarvāṅga*). On the eyes: *oṃ hāṃ*, homage to the principle of the eye (*cakṣustattva*), homage to the Lord of the principle of the eye, the Illuminator (*prakāśaka*). On the tongue: *oṃ hāṃ*, homage to the principle of the tongue (*jihvātattva*), homage to the Lord of the principle of the tongue, the Great-faced One (*mahāvaktra*).

In the nose: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the nose (nāsā-tattva). (6) To the lord of the principle of the nose, Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vilumbaka. In the mouth: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of speech (vāk-tattva); to the lord of the principle of speech, homage to Dundubhi. (p. 30a, l. 1) In the two hands: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the hand (pāṇi-tattva); to the lord of the principle of the hand, homage to Sāmadā.

At the two feet: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of the feet (*pādatattva*); salutation to Ramaṇa, the lord of the principle of the feet. (l. 2) At the anus: salutation to Tūrṇakṛt, the lord of the principle of the anus (*pāyutattva*). At the generative organ: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of the generative organ (*upasthatattva*); salutation to Ghanānanda, the lord of the principle of the generative organ.

The two mantras: *Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of sound (śabdatattva), to the lord of the principle of sound, Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the subtle resonance (sūkṣmanāda). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of touch (sparśatattva), to the lord of the principle of touch, homage to Balavaktra. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of form (rūpatattva), to the lord of the principle of form, homage to Bhānumat.*

Homage to the principle of taste; homage to the lord of the principle of taste: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jalada. (l. 6) Homage to the principle of smell; homage to the lord of the principle of smell: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gandhāṅga. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of space; homage to the lord of the principle of space, Sūkṣma. (p. 30b, l. 1) Homage to [Sūkṣma].

Salutation to the wind-principle; salutation to Mātariśvan, the lord of the wind-principle. (L. 2) Within the interior of the self-source, in the seat of bile, salutation to the fire-principle; salutation to Tviṣāṃnidhi, the lord of the fire-principle. (L. 2) From the source down to the kneecaps, salutation to the water-principle; salutation to Jaleśa, the sovereign of the water-principle.

From below the knees to the ends of the feet, [one should perform] *namaḥ pṛthvī-tattvāya* (salutation to the earth principle); *namaḥ pṛthvī-tattvādhipataye śrīkaṇṭhāya* (salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the lord of the earth principle). Having performed this placement (*nyāsa*) by including the fourteen worlds beginning with Naraka, Vāta, and Āla, immediately after the placement of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*), one should offer five oblations for each [of the five elements] according to the sequence of placement.

Having adorned [the image] with perfumes and other offerings and meditated upon its form, one should then purify the body by means of the four rites beginning with gazing (*nirīkṣaṇa*) performed with the *tathāgatagatena* mantra, and by means of the concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) and so forth. Having bathed it and worshipped the seat with the heart-mantra using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—(l. 3).

Having visualized the triad of channels—*iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*—in the left, right, and middle of the pericarp of that heart-lotus, and having contemplated the triad of powers (*śakti*)—namely Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—within them, one should deposit merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). This is for the purpose of depositing the life-force (*jīva*) into the corpse.

Having led the sound (*nāda*)—arisen by the utterance of *praṇava*—to the *dvādaśānta* with the fist [of the breath], and having conceived oneself as unified with that sound, established in one's own state, and moving from here to there according to one's own karma; [one should do so] by means of the net of the power of sound (*nādaśakti*) and the net of the power (*śaktijālikā*).

It should be visualized as pervading everywhere. Uttering the entire subtle self-mantra in the form of light, one should rotate it three times and visualize that self as the seat above it. Having grasped that self—both subtle and gross—by joining the fingers through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), [one should proceed].

Having drawn [the deity] into one's own heart with the *sṛṇī* mudrā and the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), and having divided one's own self and taken it up with the *ātma*-mantra and the *saṃhāra* mudrā; having emerged by way of the path of the flow of breath and grasped it at the *dvādaśānta*, one should join it to that [disciple's] body with the *udbhava* mudrā and cast [it] [into him].

Having offered three oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of bringing about their presence (*sānnidhya*), one should offer three oblations while contemplating: "Obeisance to the *mala*-fetters" (*malapāśebhyo namaḥ*). Having contemplated: "Obeisance to the *māyā*-fetters" (*māyāpāśebhyo namaḥ*), one should offer three oblations. Having contemplated: "Obeisance to the *karman*-fetters" (*karmapāśebhyo namaḥ*), one should offer three oblations.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *brahmans* beginning with *Sadyojāta*, the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), and the eyes; and having, in the context of the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*), performed the placement of the mantras of the *kalās* such as *Preta* and others in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*); and having placed the limbs of Śiva; one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) a thousand, half a thousand, or a hundred times with the root mantra (*mūla*) for the purpose of invoking the presence of consciousness (*caitanya-sannidhāna*).

Then, having joined the channels (*nāḍī*), one should offer three hundred oblations with the root mantra for the sake of its presence. Thereafter, having prepared a mandala on the left side of oneself, and having seated the disciple upon it, one should place the roots of *darbha* grass in the palm of the disciple’s hand with the root mantra, while holding their tips against one's own shins.

Having approached the junction (*sandhi*), one should visualize that the disciple’s channel, which resembles a lotus fiber, issues forth through the *piṅgalā* and enters one’s own channel, the *iḍā*, where it dissolves. Then, having entered by means of the *recaka* breath accompanied by the *śiva-aṇu* mantra, and [having performed] the fire-offering (*agnityāga*), one should enter the disciple’s heart by means of the *pūraka* breath.

Having exited by means of *recaka* and entered one's own heart by means of *pūraka*, one should join the channel as if with the fire on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and Śiva residing within the *kumbhaka*. For the sake of that union, one should offer three oblations for each. Then, for the purification of any deficiency in his own conduct, the initiate (*samayin*) should offer a thousand oblations with the root mantra.

[He should visualize] Rudra standing in the midst of the fire—blue-throated, three-eyed, possessing four arms, holding a trident in his hand, blazing with the mudrā of exposition, and embodying gnosis.

Having meditated upon oneself as being endowed with all ornaments and wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)—thus having visualized the self—one should join it to the seat consisting of the elements beginning with earth. Having contemplated the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth, which are produced from the mantra-seat, and the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*), which is the pure essential nature;

and having contemplated the principle of Māyā, named *bindu*, as the seat; and having formed the internal mental conception of the power of measurement (*māna-śakti*) starting from the *iṇḍikā* up to the head of the *nāda*; and with a mind one-pointed in meditation on the Supreme Lord, having visualized Śiva, whose nature is the state beyond the mind (*unmanā*).

One should unite the preceptor, who is endowed with the purification of the *sakalīkaraṇa*, with the Supreme. At the time of the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), having effected the union of the disciple’s self and one’s own mind through the wind of the *praṇava*, this is the first connection. The second connection is the meditation on the nature of the *nāda* arising from the *mūlādhāra* as the essence of the *praṇava*. The third connection is the emergence of the *nāda* through the union of the channels (*nāḍī*) for the purpose of entering the mind.

Having caused the dissolution of each respective [element] into its own right-hand [correspondence] within the six kalās—namely, the channels (*nāḍi*), the obstructions (*viṣṭava*), and those called *a*, *u*, *m*, *bindu*, *nāda*, and *nādānta*—which correspond to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Anāhataśiva, located in the places of the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, the point (*bindu*), the aperture of the skull (*biladvāra*), and the ten ends (*daśānta*).

Having dissolved time through the movement of the eyebrows while the self resides in the seventh station, the place of power (*śaktisthāna*), this is the fourth, the *praśāntaviṣuva*. Within the power (*śakti*), the sound called *nāda* should flow upward as far as the end of *samanā*. Thus, having divided the fifth, the *śaktiviṣuva*, into three parts starting from the power up to the root (*samūli*).

The subsequent time [is reached] by the emission up to the end of Śakti through a duration of sixteen *truṭis*; the further subsequent time [is reached] by the emission while contemplating through a duration consisting of seventeen *truṭis*; the further subsequent time [is reached] up to the end of Samanā through the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇācāra*) for a duration consisting of eighteen *truṭis*. Because it is the cause of dissolution (*avalaya*), this is the sixth, the Equinox of Time (*kālaviṣuva*). Then, at the end of Unmanā, there is the seventh, the Equinox of Principles (*tattvaviṣuva*) known as the Manifestor of the Self, which is the abode of Śiva existing within Unmanā. Because of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of that, one should unite the disciple—who is essentially the Supreme Śiva—beyond the partless (*niṣkala*) power of Unmanā.

Because of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the *sṛk* [the sacrificial ladle], he speaks of the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) at the equinox for the purpose of joining the disciple with the Self. Having contemplated that the *suṣumnā* channel is indeed burnt by the *sṛk*, and having contemplated the lotus of the heart as being right at the opening of the *sṛk* itself—as if it were a stream of clarified butter consisting of a flow of nectar—one should perform the visualization. Having ascertained that the disciple’s self is pervaded within the interior of the *sṛk*, immediately thereafter, with the falling of the clarified butter accompanied by the word "Śiva" and free from returning, [the teacher], joined with the supreme nectar, should utter the root mantra ending in the *nāda* while pouring down a stream of clarified butter.

One should unite the self, which has been placed within the *kumbha*, with Śiva, the presiding deity of sleep and the other states. For the sake of stability, one should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). For the sake of expiation, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *astra* mantra, one should worship the [deity] residing in the *kumbha* with flowers, and offer the *arghya* facing away.

Having joined [the deity] with Śiva residing in the fire, having worshipped that which resides in the fire with the *ṣaṭpuṣpikā* [offering], having offered the *arghya* for the one facing away, and having dismissed [the deity] with indifference, one should offer the *bali* to the enclosures and the seats. In the north: *oṃ hāṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*; in the south: *rudrāya namaḥ*; in the west: *viṣṇave namaḥ*; in the east: *brahmaṇe namaḥ*.

Having offered the *bali* at the end of the *svāhā* [mantra] with clarified butter (*ājya*), one should worship Īśāna and the others upon their seats and offer the *bali* at the end of the *svāhā*. Then, having confined the fire, one should prepare two mandalas in the area to one’s own right; in the first mandala, in the directions starting from the north and ending with the east, [one offers]: "Homage to the Yakṣas! Homage to the Gaṇas!"

Salutation to the Mothers. Salutation to the Rudras. In the corners of the northwest, southeast, and northeast, salutation to the Nāgas; salutation to the Rākṣasas; salutation to the Asuras; salutation to the Planets. In the center of the mandala, in the southwest, southeast, and northeast, salutation to the Viśvedevas; salutation to the Zodiical Signs; salutation to the Lunar Mansions.

Having worshipped with "Salutation to Kṣetrapālaka between Vāyu and Varuṇa," one should offer the *bali* ending with *svāhā*. In the second maṇḍala, having fully worshipped Īśāna and the others, one should offer the *bali* at the end of *svāhā*. In the pavilion, having offered the *arghya* facing outward according to the order of worship for the ten weapons—

Having joined [the corpse] with the *vardhanī* and bound it by means of the *pāśupatāstra*, one should then place the head of the corpse facing south upon the funeral pyre. Having covered it with a garment wrapped in the counter-clockwise direction (*apasavya*), and having maintained the form with sandalwood water and wood, the son, a relative, or a disciple—having bathed well—should take hold of it in his hand.

Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*apasavyopavītin*), having placed the water-pot upon the left shoulder, he should move counter-clockwise and, after circling three times, pour out the remaining water from which no more can flow. Having gathered the remaining water in a wooden vessel upon his shoulder, he should say: "I give this skull-water (*kapālodaka*) to the deceased [named] Śarman of [such-and-such] lineage. He should say: "I give rice for the mouth to the deceased [named] Śarmā of [such-and-such] lineage. At the location of the mouth, he should cast [the rice] with joined palms while reciting the *pitṛmantra*. Having kindled the fire with clarified butter (*ājya*), he should fill a ladle (*sruva*) with ghee, honey, milk, and curd at the region of the head.

O Agni, at this time, you must not depart from the south. Having offered a great oblation (*mahāhuti*) of clarified butter purified by mantras, and having cast the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles into the funeral pyre itself, place the *vardhanī* vessel upon your left shoulder. Having cast those who have turned away [from the world] into the state of non-appearance (*avarṇatā*) which consists of a continuous stream (*dhārāmaya*), go thereafter to a body of water without looking back. Having bathed and spread *kuśa* grass upon the ground, offer water [with the following]: "Svadhā to Skanda; svadhā to Caṇḍa; svadhā to Gaṇādhipati. This is the ritual for the final offering (*antyaṣṭi-vidhi*).
The Special Final Oblation (Viśeṣāntyeṣṭi)

The distinguished initiate, having performed everything as previously described up to the junction of all the channels (*nāḍī*) within the fire, and having worshipped Vāgīśī and Vāgīśa in the heart-lotus of the disciple, offers three oblations (*āhuti*) for each to ensure their presence. Having thus brought them together and consecrated the disciple with the *astra-mantra*, he visualizes [the deities] at the disciple’s heart-region with the *nārāca-mudrā* while reciting "Oṃ Haḥ Huṃ Phaṭ" along with flowers. Then, entering the disciple’s body through his own exhalation (*recaka*) and the syllable *Huṃ*, he separates [the disciple] from the *vijyeṣṭha* state by reciting "Oṃ Huṃ Hāṃ Huṃ Haḥ Huṃ."

Reciting "oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ svāhā" with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, one leads [the soul] to the *dvādaśānta*; having visualized the *jīva* in the form of a drop on the tip of a blade of grass, one gathers it with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* using the *ātma-mantra* ending in *namaḥ*. Having drawn it out through one's own channel (*nāḍī*) and contemplated its union with the son, one [performs this] with the *vāmā-udbhava-mudrā* using the *ātma-mantra*.

Having united [the disciple] with Vāgīśī, and having offered a hundred, a thousand, or half that number of oblations with the root mantra, one should contemplate oneself as being empowered by Śiva, the presiding lord of the state of Īśvara; then, having gratified the two lords of speech (Vāgīśa and Vāgīśī), one should dismiss them and offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Astra-mantra for the sake of expiation.

Having united the lords of the sacrificial ground with the fire, one should dismiss Śiva. Then, having placed [the body] upon the funeral pyre with its head to the south, covered it with a cloth, and ignited it with excellent fuel and flowers by means of the Śiva-fire, one should stand at the head of the corpse, hold a ladle filled with clarified butter, honey, and milk, and, uttering these words, pour out the full oblation.

Oṃ! You, O Agni, are the time of the southern period, not [otherwise]... (p. 37b, l. 1). And at the time when initiation (*dīkṣā*) is performed, it yields the most excellent fruit in the months of Phālguna and Mārgaśīrṣa; initiation in the month of Jyeṣṭha is middling; and for the sake of the lowest result, it is joyfully brought forth in Āṣāḍha and the month of Māgha, completed in Śrāvaṇa.

And likewise in Caitra, Vṛṣabha, and Bhādrapada—though these months have concluded, [the time for] initiation and the taking up [of vows] is auspicious. Indeed, at the equinoxes, the two solstices, on the day of Āṣāḍhā, during that festival, and in Uttara-bhadrapadā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Māgha, Puṣya, Punarvasu, Hasta, Svātī, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, and Rohiṇī, it is likewise [auspicious].

It is said that there are fourteen lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) that form the root of the three [types of] speech: the fourth, ninth, sixth, eighth, fourteenth, and full moon days—excluding these, the remaining days are beneficial; during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), when the stars are many, the yogas Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Dhruva, Siddhi, and Saubhāgya are favorable for one’s own form. ...and the *karaṇa* Bālava on Monday and Saturday.

The remaining [planets] are inauspicious... (l.3) ...times; likewise when the moon is lost to its auspiciousness and has set... one should not undertake an auspicious commencement or a journey by chariot. Having mastered the time and other factors, one who desires [to attain] knowledge should perform initiation (dīkṣā). (l.5) For one who seeks liberation, there is no restriction regarding the time for initiation and so forth at any time. [This concludes] the section on the constellations and the moon.

Hyavantyaśvinī is the constellation; Aśvin is the horse, the swift steed... the first. Turaṅga, turaga, aśvi, vājin, haya, and hari [are synonyms]. Bharaṇī is Yama’s, the southern, Antaka, and likewise the star of the dead. Kṛttikā is to be known as Bahulā; these six constellations belong to Hutāśana. Rohiṇī is the lotus, the body, the crown, the forest, and Vidhi.

The asterism Prājāvatya belongs to Prajeśa; Dvaidhātrya belongs to Paṅkajāsana. Mṛgaśīrṣa belongs to Vidhi; Saumya belongs to Niśā; Nadhoni belongs to Niśākara. Ārdrā belongs to Raudra; Śaṅkara [belongs to] Punarvasu. Āditya is remembered as belonging to Maṣṭhādi. Puṣya belongs to Aṅgīrasa; Tiṣya belongs to Vācaspati; Bṛhaspati [belongs to it].

Āśleṣā is known as the serpent, the cord, the snake, the adder, and the hooded one; Maghā is called the asterism of the ancestors (Pitṛbhā); [then come] Arthaman, Uttaraphalgunī, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Bhaga. Hasta is the asterism of Savitṛ and Sāvitrī; Arkasūrya is Divākara. Citrā has Tvaṣṭṛ as its deity, and Tvaṣṭṛ is the divine carpenter. Svātī is Samīraṇa, Vāyu, and Vasana... Vaiśākha is Drūpa; Indrāgnī is the dual-deity of Iṣṭāgni. Anurādhā is Maitra, Mitra, and Tāla... and Alakṣmī, Candana, and Amṛtā.
At the base, the night-stalker (Rāhu) is proclaimed; [then] Nairṛtya, Viśatāśana, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Jala, and also Udaka;
[then] Uttarāṣāḍhā, Āpya, and Viśveśa.

Śravaṇa belongs to Viṣṇu; Śrīśa and Śrīkānta are the two [lords of] Aja and Dhvajarī. Śraviṣṭhā and Dhaniṣṭhā are the Vasus, and the Vasus themselves are indeed the [deities of] the Vasu-nakṣatra. ... Prācetasa and Śatabhiṣaj are declared to belong to Varuṇa, the lord of the waters.
Ajakapāda, Ahirbudhnya, Bhadra, Bhādrapada, and likewise Uttarāproṣṭhapadā—these are known by the name Ahirbudhnya.
They say that the one immediately preceding Pauṣṇa is the last; Pūṣan is Revatī.

Having adorned [the deity] with deer-skin, garments, a crown, and so forth, and having sprinkled the sacrificial hall (*yāgagṛha*) with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and having scattered the ritual offerings (*vikirān*), one should worship the ten weapons starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and ending at the southwest (*naiṛtya*). Then, in the central jar: *oṃ hāṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ anantāsanāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*. In the corners starting from the northeast and ending at the southeast: *aiśvaryāya namaḥ*, *vairāgyāya namaḥ*, *jñānāya namaḥ*, *dharmāya namaḥ*. In the directions starting from the north and ending at the east: *anaiśvaryāya namaḥ*.

Homage to non-detachment; homage to ignorance; homage to unrighteousness. In the northeast, homage to the upper covering. In the southwest, homage to the lower covering. (Having performed this offering for the purification of the planets, then, having placed the *vardhanī* vessel upon the left shoulder with the *astra-mantra*, one should release an unbroken stream facing away, not clockwise. Having whirled it around and cast it down face-down in its own place, then, without looking back, one should go to a body of water and spread *kuśa* grass on the ground of the bank.)

One should offer nine handfuls of water with joined palms (*añjali*), reciting: *oṃ hāṃ śuddhātman skandobhava tathā...* [and] *oṃ hāṃ śuddhātman caṇḍobhava svadhā oṃ hāṃ śuddhātman gaṇādhīśobhava svadhā*. Having bathed again, they should mutter the *astra-mantra* for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

The Special Final Oblation (*viśeṣāntyeṣṭi*). In the center: *namaḥ* to the lotus, *namaḥ* to the seeds, *namaḥ* to the pericarp. In the northeast of the pericarp: *namaḥ* to Manonmanī. On the filaments from the northeast to the east: *namaḥ* to Sarvabhūtadamanī, *namaḥ* to Balapramathanī, *namaḥ* to Balavikaraṇī.

Salutation to Kalavikaraṇī; salutation to Kālī; salutation to Raudrī; salutation to Jyeṣṭhā; salutation to Vāmā. (L. 5) In the center of the pericarp, salutation to the Śakti-maṇḍala; salutation to the Lord of the Śakti-maṇḍala; salutation to Īśvara. On the circle at the tip of the pericarp, salutation to the Vahni-maṇḍala. (P. 41a, l. 1) Salutation to the Vahni-maṇḍala.

Salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala; salutation to the circle at the tips of the filaments, the moon-maṇḍala; salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the moon-maṇḍala; salutation to the sun-maṇḍala at the tips of the petals; salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the sun-maṇḍala. Above that: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Nīlakaṇṭha-Rudra; salutation to the form of Nīlakaṇṭha-Rudra. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras—Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna—from the left [side] up to the head.
Blue-throated and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted locks;
in his right hands, he holds a trident, a skull-cup, a sword, and the gesture of fearlessness.
In his left hands, he holds a serpent, an axe, a staff, and the gesture of granting boons;
he has four faces and eight arms, resplendent with a white complexion,
endowed with all ornaments, and adorned by every maṇḍala.

Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (vidyādeha)*. With flowers, filling the hollow of the hands (*añjali*) with *Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the eyes* at the faces beginning with Sadyojāta.
